newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia debt-management plan under review.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia debt-management plan under review.

text.p: British Columbia's plan to reduce the provincial debt is under review and may be revised, Premier Glen Clark said in an interview with the Vancouver Sun published Thursday.

The plan was introduced two years ago and aims to reduce the province's direct debt by C$1.3 billion by 2000. But Clark told the newspaper that it was premised on the government achieving consecutive budget surpluses. "We want to work on the debt-management plan, but the debt-management plan did call for surpluses which are not likely to occur in terms of this current year, or last year, I agree," he said.
The province said in July it had a C$235 million deficit in the fiscal year to March 31 rather than a C$16 million surplus as forecast in April.

For the current 1996/97 fiscal year the government previously forecast a C$88 million surplus. But it has backed away from that forecast, saying it will be a challenge to achieve a balanced budget this year amid weaker than expected economic growth and falling government revenues.
Government officials were not immediately available to comment on Clark's remarks. Finance Minister Andrew Petter was due to brief reporters later Thursday on cost-cutting measures.
The debt-mangement plan sought to reduce direct provincial debt to C$8.9 billion from C$10.2 billion by 1999-2000.
Clark also suggested that a freeze on capital spending projects announced this summer was being lifted.

"Every commitment we made during the election campaign and before that will be kept. Unfortunately it won't be kept as fast as we wanted, in other words over one year. Frankly we'll be building them over the next three years," he said.
Clark would not say when the buget would be balanced.
Clark announced Tuesday plans to save C$500 million per year by eliminating 3,500 civil service jobs.
The provicial government has set a goal of reducing spending by C$750 million over 18 months.

Clark's government has been under attack over its finances after accusations it deceived voters over the state of the budget. Opposition politicians claim the government withheld deficit news until after a May provincial election in which the New Democratic Party held onto to power by a slim margin.
In the first fiscal quarter to June 30, the province recorded a budget deficit of C$463 million compared to a C$228 million deficit in the same period a year earlier.
In the interview, Clark said the deadline for achieving debt reduction targets may be pushed back.

"...We clearly have to review it in light of the fact that we haven't materialized the surpluses. I'm not prepared to say we're not going to have a debt-management plan...(but) it may have to be amended, it may be a longer time frame," He said.
